\chapter{Telling Time}
\label{ch:te-telling-time}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell someone the time on the hour in Telugu, in the singular and the plural.}

Say \te{గంట} — hour, and also \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{} — then \te{ఒక} \te{గంట} for one o'clock and \te{రెండు} \te{గంటలు} for two, taking the plural -lu.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ganṭa]{\te{గంట} — matching Kannada and Hindi's \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{} word exactly}

\label{lesson:TE-C18-ganta}



\begin{quote}
Telugu completes a clean three-way match: Hindi, Kannada, and now Telugu all use the same Sanskrit \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{} word for \textquotedblleft{}hour.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గంట} — bell AND hour, a third time}
\textbf{\te{గంట}} (\emph{ganṭa}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{hour}\textquotedblright{} — and, exactly like Hindi's \emph{ghanṭā} and Kannada's \emph{gaṇṭe}, it means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{bell, clapper}\textquotedblright{} just as commonly, from the same Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{घण्टा}} (\emph{ghaṇṭā}). Same word, same bell-strikes-the-hour logic, three languages in a row.

\begin{culture}
So on this concept, the split isn't \textquotedblleft{}Hindi vs. all four Dravidian languages\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{Hindi, Kannada, and Telugu} all share the Sanskrit \emph{ghaṇṭā} (\textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{}) root. \textbf{Tamil} most likely goes its own way with a native Dravidian word instead (though even specialists don't call this fully settled). \textbf{Malayalam} is the genuinely surprising one: its cognate word, \emph{mani}, is ALSO Sanskrit-derived per its own dictionaries — just from a \textbf{different} Sanskrit word, \emph{maṇi} (\textquotedblleft{}gem\textquotedblright{}), not \emph{ghaṇṭā}. So three of these four languages likely trace their hour-word to Sanskrit, just not all to the \emph{same} Sanskrit word — worth remembering that a Sanskrit/native split isn't fixed per language, and isn't always a clean binary either.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: telling the time}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{ఒక} \te{గంట}.} — \textquotedblleft{}One o'clock.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{oka ganṭa}, \textquotedblleft{}one hour/bell\textquotedblright{}) \textbf{\te{రెండు} \te{గంటలు}.} — \textquotedblleft{}Two o'clock.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{reṇḍu ganṭalu} — \emph{ganṭa} takes its plural form, \emph{ganṭalu}, once the count passes one)
\end{quote}

Notice Telugu's \emph{ganṭa} pluralizes to \emph{ganṭalu} for \textquotedblleft{}two o'clock\textquotedblright{} onward — a small grammatical wrinkle Kannada's \emph{gaṇṭe} didn't show you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ganṭa\textquotedblright{} — hour, also \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}oka ganṭa\textquotedblright{} — one o'clock
  \item \textquotedblleft{}reṇḍu ganṭalu\textquotedblright{} — two o'clock, plural \emph{ganṭalu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit word do \textbf{\te{గంట}}, Kannada's \emph{gaṇṭe}, and Hindi's \emph{ghanṭā} all share? (\textbf{\dv{घण्टा}}, \emph{ghaṇṭā}, \textquotedblleft{}bell.\textquotedblright{}) Which Dravidian language most likely does NOT use this Sanskrit word for \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Tamil} — most likely a native Dravidian word instead.) Does Malayalam's cognate word skip Sanskrit entirely too? (\textbf{No} — it's Sanskrit-derived too, per its own dictionaries, just from a \emph{different} Sanskrit word, \emph{maṇi}, \textquotedblleft{}gem.\textquotedblright{}) What happens to \emph{ganṭa} for \textquotedblleft{}two o'clock\textquotedblright{}? (It \textbf{pluralizes} to \emph{ganṭalu}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ḷa]{\te{ళ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S121-letter-lla}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌ే} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ళ}}
\textbf{\te{ళ}} — \emph{ḷa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ḷ}, it is \textbf{ḷa}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{ళ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళు}} \emph{veḷḷu} — to go (and \te{వచ్చు}, to come)
  \item \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళి} \te{వస్తాను}} \emph{veḷḷi vastānu} — goodbye (lit. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{మళ్ళీ} \te{కలుద్దాం}} \emph{maḷḷī kaluddām} — we'll meet again
  \item \textbf{\te{సోమవారం} \te{మంగళవారం} \te{బుధవారం} \te{గురువారం} \te{శుక్రవారం} \te{శనివారం} \te{ఆదివారం}} — the seven weekdays
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{ళ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{ళ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{ళ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{వెళ్ళు}  ·  \te{నమస్కారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{ళ} three times, saying \emph{ḷa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{ళ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{ళ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ḷa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
